nodes.name: Tulip-tree
nodes.desc: A tall hardwood of moist Appalachian forests; its leaves feed the caterpillars of the eastern tiger swallowtail.

nodes.name: American beech
nodes.desc: A hardwood whose nuts (beechnuts) are eaten by black bears, squirrels and other forest animals.

nodes.name: Eastern hemlock
nodes.desc: A shade-tolerant conifer of moist ravines and hillsides, part of the hemlock-hardwood forest. Introduced woolly adelgids threaten it.

nodes.name: Great laurel
nodes.desc: A dominant evergreen understory shrub of moist Appalachian slopes and streamsides that forms dense thickets and gives shelter to wildlife.

nodes.name: Orange jewelweed
nodes.desc: A moisture-loving wildflower of seeps and streambanks; GloBI records groundhogs and cottontails eating it.

nodes.name: White-tailed deer
nodes.desc: The park's most recorded large mammal. It browses shoots, leaves, nuts and herbs, and heavy browsing can slow tree regrowth.

nodes.name: Eastern chipmunk
nodes.desc: A ground-dwelling squirrel that eats nuts and seeds and is itself prey for many predators.

nodes.name: Eastern gray squirrel
nodes.desc: A tree squirrel of hardwood forests that eats nuts and seeds such as beechnuts.

nodes.name: Eastern cottontail
nodes.desc: A rabbit of forest edges and clearings that eats herbs and is prey for foxes, coyotes and snakes.

nodes.name: Groundhog
nodes.desc: A burrowing rodent that eats green plants and is eaten by coyotes, foxes and bears.

nodes.name: Eastern Tiger Swallowtail
nodes.desc: A large butterfly whose caterpillars feed on tulip-tree and other hardwood leaves.

nodes.name: Raccoon
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats small mammals, birds, amphibians, fruit and more; GloBI has many prey records.

nodes.name: Eastern Rat Snake
nodes.desc: A big constrictor that eats rodents, rabbits and birds.

nodes.name: Timber rattlesnake
nodes.desc: A venomous ambush hunter of rocky forest that eats chipmunks, squirrels, rabbits and other small animals.

nodes.name: Red fox
nodes.desc: A small canid that hunts rabbits, rodents and birds. Coyotes may prey on it.

nodes.name: Turkey vulture
nodes.desc: A scavenging bird that cleans up carcasses of deer and other animals and is very well recorded in the area.

nodes.name: Coyote
nodes.desc: Now the main wild predator of deer fawns and small mammals in much of the East, where wolves and cougars have been lost.

nodes.name: Black bear
nodes.desc: An omnivore: mostly plants and nuts such as beechnuts, plus insects, carrion and sometimes deer fawns.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Light reaching the forest floor limits how much understory and wildflowers can grow beneath the canopy.

nodes.name: Rain & humidity
nodes.desc: Wet, humid air keeps ravines moist for hemlock and rhododendron.

nodes.name: New River & streams
nodes.desc: Water carved the gorge, and the riparian zone is the park's most biologically diverse area.

nodes.name: Forest soil
nodes.desc: Leaf litter and rotting wood break down into nutrients that trees and wildflowers take up.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi, bacteria and invertebrates that recycle fallen leaves, wood and carcasses.
